prompt: The state object was deleted. What happened to the resources it described?
hint: The state is a record, not the resources.

choices.text: They were deleted with the state, in the same request
choices.why: Deleting an object in S3 touches that object only.

choices.text: They are marked for deletion at the next apply
choices.why: The next plan wants to create them, not delete them.

choices.text: Nothing: they still exist and keep serving
choices.why: Right. Terraform forgot them; AWS did not.

choices.text: They stop working until the state is restored
choices.why: Resources never consult the state; only Terraform does.

prompt: After the state was lost, the apply adopted the SNS topic without an error but failed on the bucket. Why the difference?
hint: What does each service answer to a create of a name that exists?

choices.text: Creating an existing topic returns it; a bucket refuses
choices.why: Right. SNS answers with the existing topic, S3 with BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou.

choices.text: The topic was newer than the bucket
choices.why: Age plays no part; the services answer differently.

choices.text: Terraform retries topics but not buckets
choices.why: No retry was involved; the first call succeeded for the topic.

choices.text: The bucket had DeletionPolicy Retain
choices.why: That is CloudFormation; this bucket is Terraform's, and the policy says nothing about creation.

prompt: With the state lost, which kind of resource is the most dangerous for an apply to recreate?
hint: What stops a second copy from being made?

choices.text: A bucket, because its name is global
choices.why: The global name is what makes the create fail, which is the safe outcome.

choices.text: A log group, because its logs are lost
choices.why: The create fails on the existing name, and the logs stay where they are.

choices.text: An SNS topic, because it is adopted
choices.why: Adoption leaves one topic; it is quiet, but no copy is made.

choices.text: One with no unique name, such as an EC2 instance
choices.why: Right. The create succeeds, and the account holds two, one of them unmanaged.

prompt: What does deleting an object in a versioned bucket actually do?

choices.text: Removes the newest version only
choices.why: A plain delete removes no version; it hides them behind a marker.

choices.text: Adds a delete marker on top of the versions
choices.why: Right. Earlier versions stay readable by their ids.

choices.text: Moves the object to a recycle bucket for 30 days
choices.why: S3 has no recycle bucket; the versions stay in the same bucket.

choices.text: Removes every version unless MFA delete is on
choices.why: Versions are only removed by deleting each one by id.

prompt: The history shows an 8,403-byte version, a delete marker one second later, and a 2,744-byte version after that. Which version is restored?
hint: The last good one, before the marker.

choices.text: The 2,744-byte one, because it is the latest
choices.why: It was written by the bad apply and records one resource.

choices.text: The delete marker, by deleting it
choices.why: Removing the marker exposes the 2,744-byte version, the newest one beneath it.

choices.text: The 8,403-byte one, from before the marker
choices.why: Right. It holds the four resources, and copying it makes it the latest.

choices.text: Neither: a version cannot be restored once a newer one exists
choices.why: Any version can be copied on top, whatever came after.

prompt: Why stop every pipeline before restoring the state?
hint: Look at where the 2,744-byte version came from.

choices.text: Because S3 refuses copy-object while a lock exists
choices.why: S3 knows nothing of Terraform's lock; the copy would succeed.

choices.text: Because versioning is suspended during a restore
choices.why: Versioning stays on; the restore itself is a new version.

choices.text: Because pipelines cache the state and would overwrite it at once
choices.why: Pipelines read the state fresh each run; the risk is a run happening, not a cache.

choices.text: An apply in between writes a newer, wrong version
choices.why: Right. That is exactly how the bad version appeared.

prompt: The good state version is 8,403 bytes and the bad one 2,744. How many bytes larger is the good one?
When is an `import` block the way out, rather than a restore?

choices.text: When no version or copy of the state is left
choices.why: Right. With a version or a pulled copy, restoring is faster.

choices.text: When the resources were deleted as well
choices.why: Import needs the resources to exist; a deleted one is created again instead.

choices.text: Whenever the plan shows changes
choices.why: Changes are ordinary; import is for resources the state does not know.

choices.text: Only for resources created in the console
choices.why: Any existing resource can be imported, whoever made it.

prompt: What should be done with the file `-generate-config-out` writes?
hint: It describes the resource as it is.

choices.text: Commit it as it is, since Terraform wrote it
choices.why: It restates every default and copies the resource's mistakes along with it.

choices.text: Delete it after the apply, because the state is enough
choices.why: Without resource blocks, the next plan would destroy the imported resources.

choices.text: Read it, trim defaults, compare with intent
choices.why: Right. It is a draft of what exists, which may not be what was meant.

choices.text: Run it through cfn-lint
choices.why: cfn-lint reads CloudFormation templates, not HCL.

prompt: Match what is left after the accident to the way out.

pairs.left: A version of the state in the bucket
A file from terraform state pull

prompt: To have Terraform write resource blocks for imported resources, run `terraform plan -generate-___-out=generated.tf`.
The bucket policy denies `s3:DeleteObject` on `*.tfstate` except to one role. Why are the `.tflock` objects not blocked too?
hint: Terraform deletes one of them on every run.

choices.text: Lock files are not stored in the bucket
choices.why: With use_lockfile they are, beside the state.

choices.text: The resource pattern ends in .tfstate, and they end in .tflock
choices.why: Right. Blocking them would break every run, which deletes its lock at the end.

choices.text: Explicit denies never apply to small objects
choices.why: Size plays no part in a policy.

choices.text: Terraform uses the maintenance role to delete them
choices.why: Terraform runs as whoever runs it, not as the maintenance role.

prompt: Which habits protect against losing the state? Choose all that apply.
hint: Fewer deleters, a longer history, a second copy.

choices.text: terraform state pull before anything unusual
choices.why: Yes. A copy that does not depend on the bucket.

choices.text: Editing the state object by hand when a value is wrong
choices.why: No. Hand edits skip the lock and the serial; use the state subcommands.

choices.text: An alert when a state object is deleted
choices.why: Yes. CloudTrail data events can record it.

choices.text: One state for every environment, to keep it simple
choices.why: No. One accident would then cost every environment at once.

choices.text: Noncurrent versions kept longer than it takes to notice
choices.why: Yes. The history has to outlast the discovery.

prompt: Put the recovery from a deleted state object in order.
hint: Stop the damage, find, restore, confirm.
items: Stop every pipeline and person that could apply
List the object's versions and delete markers
Copy the last good version on top
Run terraform plan and expect no changes
trap: Restoring before stopping the pipelines is the slip: a run in between writes a newer bad version.

prompt: A plan on a quiet Tuesday says `Plan: 4 to add` for a configuration that has run for a year. What do you do first?
hint: A plan that wants to create what exists is about the state.

choices.text: Apply it, since Terraform knows best
choices.why: Applying adopts some, fails on others, and may duplicate the rest.

choices.text: Stop, and check the state object and its history
choices.why: Right. The plan is telling you the state is missing, not the resources.

choices.text: Run terraform destroy to start clean
choices.why: With an empty state, destroy finds nothing, and the plan problem remains.

choices.text: Delete the four resources by hand so the plan is right
choices.why: That turns a lost record into an outage.
